subtitle: Q1 Updates on Three Asian Value Setups
title: Boring Is Beautiful
description: Q1 Updates on Three Asian Value Setups
body_html:

It’s been a busy earnings season and I wanted to share a brief update on two existing value positions that delivered excellent earnings, as well as a new position in Korea.

1. For Startups (7089 JT Equity)

I featured For Startups as a new position in the April 2026 Portfolio Review as Idea 3, "Capital Light in Japan" (Entry Price: 1,224 Yen). For Startup’s Q1 Earnings report (released on Friday), was excellent, and I think its 30% top-line growth and significant guidance upgrade are likely to finally get it some attention. Before I get into the results, I want to briefly summarize the story.

For Startups is perhaps the most Japanese company you can imagine, a Venture Fund, a Database of startups, and a Headhunter all in one. What it truly represents, however, is a pure play way to ride the wave of exploding Japanese VC Activity in a capital-light vehicle.

For Startups has significant ties to leading Japanese VCs such as M3, Incubate Fund KK, Globis Capital Partners, Wil LLC, Strike Co, and Sparx Group (who are also shareholders in the company). For Startups specializes in placing C-level executives and technology employees across startups, and leverages its close ties to existing Japanese VCs and its proprietary startup database (Startup DB Japan) to identify companies in need of its services. The company also has a small co-invest portfolio that it invests alongside its VC clients, while the portfolio is not meaningful at 600 Million Yen (less than 10% of the market cap), the combination of its Startup DB, the co-invest portfolio, and its close ties to leading VCs has created a massive referral base: when VCs have portfolio companies that need to hire, they just call For Startups.

The company has been riding the wave of increasing startup activity in Japan, and earnings have steadily grown from 22 Yen in 2021 to 99 Yen in 2025, a CAGR of 45%. The CEO, Yuichiro Shimizu, has routinely highlighted he believes the shares are undervalued, and in addition to pulling 2027 guidance forward one year, the company repurchased 160,000 shares (roughly 4% of the float) in March.

For Startup’s incredible earnings report (released last Friday) has caught my eye. Revenue for the first quarter of 2026 was up a stunning 63% year over year, and earnings per share jumped 80% (to 55 Yen per share), demonstrating the company’s significant operating leverage and capital-light nature. Unlike many Japanese companies who trade at low multiples due to heavy investment needs to remain competitive and a general inability to return capital, For Startups is the exact opposite: its headhunting business is inherently capital-light, and the company continues to opportunistically pursue share repurchases while still generating 50% top-line growth.

The company’s investor presentation (which is astutely posted in English to attract US attention) has guided significant growth for 2026: revenue growth of 25%, and 145 Yen in Earnings per Share (38% growth).

(Source: Company Filings)

I think For Startups has all the markings of a “capital light compounder” aside from a migraine inducing multiple and the usual circle of GARP lovers who only get interested in 6% growth once it’s already trading at 30x earnings. I think the recent first quarter results and full year guidance upgrade to 145 Yen in EPS confirms the thesis I had last month: For Startups has positioned itself as an indispensable headhunter for the Japanese Startup industry, and will continue to ride the wave of elevated business investment. Quarterly headhunting placements are soaring, the company is increasingly focused on high ticket (salary) roles, and its Startup DB division is generating record annual recurring revenue.

For Startups excels in meeting my value investment criteria. The company specializes in catering to an under-served niche, has a clean balance sheet with a strong net cash position (approximately 330 Yen per share), has extremely aligned insiders who own 20% of the company, and is capital-light in nature, making it easy for the company to return cash to the shareholders.

With guidance for 145 Yen in earnings in 2026, I think the company is too cheap to ignore at 1,359 Yen, and that the combination of 30% guided earnings growth, a capital-light business, and the management team’s consistent history of execution, may warrant a 11x - 14x multiple, which would imply upside to 1,595 - 2,030 Yen a share.

The next two names are below a paywall for a very simple reason: both trade at deep discounts to Tangible Book Value, and are actively conducting highly accretive share repurchases. It’s a bit paradoxical, but the cheaper these stocks remain, the more value is created for long-term shareholders when management is able to repurchase stock at 5x earnings. If you have zero interest in Asian value investing, don’t subscribe. I can assure you both of these pitches are exceedingly boring, and you may even fall asleep at your desk if you read further.

2. SE Holdings and Incubations (9478 JT Equity)

SE Holdings and Incubations announced another excellent quarter on Friday. Tangible Book Value per share grew from 696 Yen to 732 Yen in the quarter, driven by steady gains from its sizeable Securities Portfolio.

For those unfamiliar with the name (larger write up here), SE is a holding company with operations in publishing, marketing, software development, and educational services, but its real gem is its Securities Portfolio, which is larger than the entire market cap of the company (approximately 774 Yen in Securities per share). It’s a picturesque net-net in the truest sense.

Unlike many other Japanese value traps who appear optically cheap but pay little attention to shareholder returns, SE Holdings and Incubations regularly uses the dividends and interest generated by its sizeable Investment Portfolio to repurchase shares. In fact, of all Japanese listed equities, SE Holdings has reduced shares outstanding by the largest percent over the last 3 years. It’s quite an accomplishment for a company no one has ever heard of.

The steady cadence of share repurchases, and rising equity markets (S&P, Topix, and HSI), has driven consistent growth in Tangible Book Value per share, yet the stock still trades at just 487 Yen (0.66x Tangible Book), implying 50% upside.

The discount is even larger when considering equity markets are up massively since the end of the first quarter. As of today, the Topix is up 9%, the HSI is up 7%, and the S&P 500 is up 14% since March 31st, which will provide a significant tailwind to Q2 results due to the Securities Portfolio.

What I like about SE Holdings is its slow and steady approach. It doesn’t announce massive dividends or significant share repurchases - instead, like clockwork, it initiates small share repurchases for 3-4% of the float after every earnings report. These repurchases are just enough to create value and stabilize the stock, but small enough to evade the usual circle of Japanese investors who run wild when spotting bargains. Just this past Friday, SE announced a fresh authorization for up to 160 Million Yen or 400,000 shares between May 11th and June 19th, which implies the company will be in the market for roughly 3.3% of the float over the next month.

I’m bullish on Japanese equities, and 9478 remains my preferred way to get exposure at a deep discount to Net Asset Value. I don’t expect the discount to close anytime soon, given SE’s small market cap and thin liquidity, but the share repurchases at 0.66x Tangible Book are highly accretive and generate significant value for the remaining long-term shareholders. Unlike most publicly listed closed end funds (such as the recent IPO PSUS), who trade at sizeable discounts to Net Asset Value because of significant fees and a general aversion to share repurchases, SE Holdings and Incubations is the exact opposite: it has a profitable publishing business that covers all its overhead, and it regularly acquires 10-15% of the float a year.

I think SE Holdings represents a rare opportunity to get exposure to Japanese equities at a significant discount. I consider SE Holdings to be a “tuck away” position: it’s not incredibly exciting, but the value is highly compelling and its exemplary capital allocation is poised to continue driving excellent returns for long-term shareholders. I think even a small position provides an opportunity to add deep-value torque to your portfolio, and that you can comfortably hold the name long-term unless it ever begins trading at a premium to Tangible Book Value, which I believe is unlikely to occur anytime soon. I believe that SE Holdings will eventually achieve 0.75x Tangible Book Value, which should imply 577 Yen a share assuming market valuations remain steady for the rest of the quarter.

3. Hyundai Green Food (453340 KS Equity)

Hyundai Green Food is an integrated food company specializing in Institutional catering and food ingredient delivery, and serves over 700,000 meals a day across 600 domestic and 100 International sites (hospitals, corporate kitchens, factories).

The company was spunoff from Hyundai GF Holdings (similar name, but operates Department stores, diners, furniture, heavy machinery, leasing, what a mix) and began trading in March 2023. Prior to the spinoff, the sticky nature of the foodservice business was difficult to distinguish given it was simply a division of a much larger holding company. Since the spinoff, the company has made steady progress in improving shareholder relations, expanding margins at its Hyundai locations (now that it is independent) and most importantly, adopting shareholder-first capital allocation, and investors are finally beginning to notice.

Hyundai Green Food’s expansion into “health conscious” catering via its “Greeting” brand, which specializes in high protein or low sugar meals for those with diabetes and other health issues, is growing nearly 20% a year. Gross margin has grown from 16.5% in 2023, to 17.6% in 2024 and 18.0% in 2025, and 2025 earnings came in at 2,654 Won, a record.

The company’s recent Q1 earnings report tells a story of inflecting growth and significant operating leverage: revenue jumped 9% and operating profit rose 44% as the company’s expansion into health-conscious meals and hospitals drives significant incremental earnings with minimal investment required. More importantly, the company has now established a concrete plan to return capital: the 10 Billion Won dividend will double to 20 Billion Won by 2028, and the company also intends to cancel 10% of shares outstanding (3.2 Million) by 2028.

Hyundai Green Food currently trades at 19,200 Won, a small discount to Tangible Book Value of 19,500 Won. Importantly, the company has a Net Cash per Share position of 4,800 Won, and capital expenditures have remained steady over the last 5 years, making it extremely easy for the company to divert a portion of its growing earnings stream to the shareholders.

The 370 Won dividend (1.90% yield) is on track to become 700 Won within two years (3.60% implied yield) and the company is steadily repurchasing 5,000 shares a day, which is significant given just 14 Million shares are circulating (by the end of the year, the company will have acquired approximately 9% of the float). Given the impressive Q1 results, the company is likely trading at just 5.5x forward earnings, which I think is even more astounding when considering the company trades at a discount to Tangible Book value and has a sizeable cash pile. The food service industry in Korea is stable, and giants such as Hyundai Green Food are unlikely to face significant competition from peers such as Samsung Welstory, as end customers such as Hyundai subsidiaries are unlikely to prefer working with another Chaebol over their own affiliate.

While the stock is up 16% in the last week, I think the move is warranted. Many Japanese and Korean names continue to languish because they have significant cash on their balance sheet or earnings, but the management teams have no interest in returning that value to the shareholders. I think in this case, Hyundai Green Food’s impressive Q1 results, paired with a shareholder-friendly capital return plan, justify the recent rally.

Even after this move, I believe Hyundai Green Food is still too cheap to ignore at 5.5x forward earnings, especially for a business that has demonstrated steady bottom line growth of 10%, and clear capital allocation intentions. I find the long-term prospects attractive: either the stock hovers in the current 16,000 - 19,000 Won range (4.8 - 5.5x earnings) and the share repurchases create additional value, or the stock eventually re-rates to 7x earnings, which would imply upside to 25,000 Won a share. Given the recent move up, I’ve purchased half my ideal position in the 19,000’s, and have left room to add the rest in the 18,000’s, should the rally the retrace.

Conclusion

None of these names are likely to dominate headlines. They don’t carry the excitement of Chips, AI Infrastructure, or a Hidden “Bottleneck”, but that’s precisely why I like them. In a market where attention is concentrated in maybe a dozen names (after reading this I’m sure three popped into your head), I think it makes sense to add small positions unrelated to AI, where the value exists in plain sight. The setups are extremely straightfoward: we don’t need For Startups to magically become the next Recuit Holdings, or SE Holdings and Incubations to make a brilliant and daring Intel Options trade no one else saw. All we need is for the steady stream of earnings to continue, and for that cash to be returned via dividends and repurchases.

These names are less liquid than my average position, but I think the lower liquidity is the main reason they trade at attractive valuations. If For Startups were a Billion dollar company I’d doubt it would be trading under 10x earnings, and if SE Holdings were slightly larger it probably would’ve been bought by an activist a while ago. Still, I think there is a price for everything, and that a diversified basket of Japanese and Korean value names at small weight provides an opportunity to add “torque” to your portfolio at extremely attractive multiples, while avoiding single name concentration risk. I continue to think Korea and Japan are “prime time” for finding cash heavy, inexpensive names with improving capital allocation and will have more ideas in the future, but I think for now, these three are worth adding to your watchlists.
